title: Unconditional subexponential simulation of BPP
formal:
Is \(\mathrm{BPP}\subseteq\mathrm{SUBEXP}\) unconditionally? Here the subexponential class is the intersection
\[\mathrm{SUBEXP}=\bigcap_{k\ge1}\mathrm{DTIME}\!\left(2^{n^{1/k}}\right).\]
Thus, for every language \(L\subseteq\{0,1\}^{*}\) decidable with two-sided bounded error in randomized polynomial time, and for every integer \(k\ge1\), must there exist a deterministic algorithm deciding \(L\) on every input in time \(O(2^{n^{1/k}})\)? The algorithm and the constant in its time bound may depend on \(L,k\). The target selects the subexponential question in the source's Open Problem 3.4; its separate quasipolynomial-time question is stronger.
why: This asks whether randomness can provide a much larger speedup than the usual derandomization conjectures predict, even after allowing deterministic time far beyond polynomial. An unconditional simulation would move the general worst-case upper bound into the source’s much smaller subexponential class. A counterexample would establish a major separation between randomized and deterministic computation.

sentences: BPP contains decision problems solved efficiently using random bits with bounded error on every input.
The question asks whether all of them have exact deterministic simulations in the class SUBEXP.
Here SUBEXP requires a simulation in time two to the n-to-epsilon power for every fixed positive epsilon.
The simulator may depend on the chosen exponent, but it must work on every input without advice or assumptions.
Known general brute-force simulations take larger exponential time, while stronger derandomization theorems rely on unproved hardness.

definitions:
A language is a set of finite binary strings. An algorithm decides \(L\) if it halts and outputs one exactly on inputs in \(L\), and zero on all other inputs. Use uniform multitape Turing machines with finite descriptions independent of input length. One transition costs one time unit. A randomized machine may additionally request independent unbiased bits, at unit cost per bit. It has no advice, oracle or preprocessing that depends on input length without being computed by the machine.

Membership in \(\mathrm{BPP}\) means that there are such a randomized machine \(M\) and constants \(a,C\ge1\) with worst-case runtime at most \(C(n+1)^a\) on every length-\(n\) input and every random tape, and with
\[x\in L\Rightarrow\Pr[M(x)=1]\ge2/3,\qquad x\notin L\Rightarrow\Pr[M(x)=1]\le1/3.\]
This is a class of total decision problems. The acceptance-probability gap holds on every input; it is not a promise that an external user must supply.

The notation \(L\in\mathrm{DTIME}(2^{n^{1/k}})\) means that a deterministic machine decides \(L\) and has worst-case runtime at most \(C_k\lceil2^{n^{1/k}}\rceil\) for all sufficiently large \(n\), for some fixed \(C_k\). All finitely many smaller inputs must also be decided correctly and with termination. Requiring every integer \(k\) is equivalent to requiring time \(O(2^{n^\varepsilon})\) for every fixed real \(\varepsilon>0\). The machine is allowed to change with the exponent; an effective compiler taking \(M,k\) and producing the simulator is not an additional requirement.

This definition of SUBEXP is the source's intersection of subpower-exponential time classes. A single \(2^{o(n)}\)-time bound, such as \(2^{n/\log n}\), need not meet it. Likewise, correctness only on most inputs, or on infinitely many input lengths, is insufficient. The simulator must decide the same language exactly on all strings.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of the inclusion or its negation. A positive proof must cover every BPP language and every fixed exponent \(1/k\), without a hardness assumption, oracle or advice. A negative proof must establish a language in BPP that is outside one of the deterministic time classes in the displayed intersection. A conditional simulation, a simulation for a particular randomized problem, or a heuristic correct on almost all inputs does not settle the question.

context_blocks.text: Enumerating every random tape gives a deterministic simulation in \(2^{\mathrm{poly}(n)}\) time. A polynomial-time randomized algorithm can use polynomially many random bits, so this direct simulation gives EXP rather than the displayed SUBEXP target.
If \(\mathrm{BPP}=\mathrm P\), the desired inclusion follows. The converse is not asserted: a subexponential simulator may still take much more than polynomial time.

Known hardness-versus-randomness theorems yield much stronger derandomization under suitable circuit lower-bound assumptions. For example, the Impagliazzo–Wigderson theorem derives BPP = P from exponential circuit hardness for a language computable in single-exponential time. Those hardness hypotheses are part of the conditional theorem and cannot be removed by citing it.

Fixing a good random tape separately for each length gives a nonuniform object. Uniformity requires a finite deterministic algorithm that computes its behavior; a sequence of good tapes supplied for free does not meet the target.
